solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Spots leaving head with second rash

indicators.note: when something leaves its head, the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: small brown spots on the skin
S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: Someone notices a spotty outbreak spreading from their head, followed by a second rash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' and 'rash' both seem medical, but the spots are freckles and the rash is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Rash and reckless are synonyms, both describing behaviour done without thinking about danger or consequences.

clue.text: Celebrate unsurpassed performance

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to mark an occasion by setting it down for posterity
second meaning: a best-ever result, such as a world best

explanation.surface: Fans are urged to cheer a performance nobody has ever bettered.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to commemorate or mark an event; as a noun it is the best result ever achieved.

clue.text: Company removes rogue and makes impression

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company

indicators.note: rogue means behaving out of control, so the letters of removes run wild into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A firm sacks a rogue employee and wins people over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Removes rogue' reads as a firm getting rid of a crook; 'rogue' is the anagram signal working on 'removes'.
explanation.definitionFit: To come over as confident is to give that impression to others, so the phrasal verb means making an impression.

clue.text: Comparatively loud den of beasts on island to the north

parts.note: a lair is a wild animal's den

indicators.note: in a down clue going north means reading upwards, so the pair of words is written backwards

parts.note: re means on or about, as in a letter heading
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: The roaring from an animal's den on a northern island grows noisier.
explanation.walkthrough: Lairy is British slang for flashy or loud and aggressive.
explanation.definitionFit: Lairy means garish or showily loud, so its comparative form describes something more vulgar and brash than another.

clue.text: Son manipulated person's issue

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
a pawn is someone used by others for their own ends

explanation.surface: A son who was used by others has a grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Person's issue' looks like a problem someone has; the apostrophe s stands for 'is', and issue means offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue is a formal word for offspring or descendants, and spawn is a scornful word for children.

clue.text: Register to enter prize competition for jam

indicators.note: one thing entering another goes inside it, so the register is placed within the prize

parts.note: a cup is both a trophy and a competition played for one, like the FA Cup
a log is a written record or register

explanation.surface: Someone signs up to take part in a contest whose prize is a jar of jam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jam' looks like a preserve offered as a prize; here it is the verb meaning to block.
explanation.definitionFit: To jam a pipe or road is to block it so nothing can pass, which is what clogging up does.

clue.text: Had food sent out with article missing

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so the article is taken out of the word for sent out

parts.note: to launch a ship or rocket is to send it out
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Someone ate a takeaway meal delivered with one item absent from the order.
explanation.definitionFit: To lunch is to eat a midday meal, so the past tense fits the phrase meaning ate.

clue.text: Despair of game, being pinned by Grand Master

indicators.note: something pinned is held fast between two holders, so the game sits between the grand and master letters

parts.note: G is short for grand, a thousand pounds
loo is an old card game
M is the abbreviation for master

explanation.surface: A chess player despairs at being pinned by a Grandmaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand Master' looks like the chess title, but it splits into two abbreviations. Loo is also British slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloom is a state of sadness and hopelessness, so it is a synonym for despair.

clue.text: Poster oddly containing goddess mounted on Eastern dog

indicators.note: containing means holding inside, so the kept poster letters wrap around the rest
oddly means keep the odd-numbered letters: the first, third and fifth of poster

parts.note: the odd letters of poster

indicators.note: in a down clue on means sitting above, so the goddess comes before the Eastern letter
in a down clue mounted means going up, so the goddess's name is read from the bottom

parts.note: Nike is the Greek goddess of victory
E is the abbreviation for Eastern

explanation.surface: A poster shows a goddess riding an oriental dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Pekinese, also spelt Pekingese, is a small long-haired breed from China.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pekinese is a breed of toy dog originally kept in the Chinese imperial palace at Peking.

clue.text: Fruit mass that is fed to horse

indicators.note: food fed to an animal goes into it, so the pair of short pieces goes inside the horse

parts.note: a pinto is a piebald or patchy horse
M is the abbreviation for mass in physics
ie is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A large quantity of fruit is given to a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' looks like a quantity of fruit, but it is just the physics abbreviation, and 'fed to' sends the pieces into the middle of the horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A pimiento is a sweet red pepper, botanically a fruit, often stuffed into olives.

clue.text: Search people following one group avoiding fine security device

indicators.note: avoiding something means keeping away from it, so the fine abbreviation is left out of the group word
following means coming after, so the people word is placed after the word for one

parts.note: to comb an area is to search it thoroughly
I is the Roman numeral for one
a nation is a people
a flock is a group, of sheep or of churchgoers
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: Police search a crowd, tracking a lone member of a gang who dodges a fine.
explanation.definitionFit: A combination lock is a security device opened by setting a sequence of numbers rather than using a key.

clue.text: This foreigner messing with Kyiv could be risky with vain US

indicators.note: messing with something jumbles it, so the solution's letters are mixed together with the city's
could be says the mixed letters may be rearranged as the longer phrase, so taking the city back out leaves the solution's letters

parts.note: the Ukrainian capital, taken as written
taken as written: the letters that the answer and the city together make

explanation.surface: A foreign power interfering with Ukraine's capital is warned that its actions are dangerous, in the company of a vain America.
explanation.walkthrough: A compound anagram: RUSSIAN plus KYIV can be rearranged into RISKY VAIN US, so removing KYIV's letters from that phrase leaves RUSSIAN to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A Russian is a national of Russia, a foreigner from the point of view of the British solver.

clue.text: Savage on good terms with barbarian hugging mother

parts.note: to be in with someone is to be on good terms with them

indicators.note: hugging means wrapping arms around, so the barbarian word surrounds the mother word

parts.note: the Huns were barbarian invaders of the Roman Empire
an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A wild man is friendly with a barbarian who is hugging his mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Savage behaviour is cruel and brutal, lacking the compassion expected of decent people, so inhuman fits as an adjective.

clue.text: Anybody mighty stops handle turning

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so the mighty word sits inside as a stopper would
turning round makes the word for handle face the other way

parts.note: a handle is slang for a name
mighty is an informal intensifier, as in mighty good, meaning very

explanation.surface: Anyone powerful enough can stop a door handle from turning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handle' looks like a door fitting but is slang for a name. Everyman is also the name of a long-running Observer crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyman means the ordinary person, anybody at all, as in the old morality play character who stands for all humanity.

clue.text: Tree hit over shed in moving earth around

indicators.note: around suggests letters being moved about into a different arrangement
when a word is over and shed in another, its letters are thrown off and gone from that phrase

parts.note: taken as written: the letters to remove
taken as written

explanation.surface: A falling tree crashes onto a garden shed while the ground shifts around it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' wants to be the anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder: take the letters of HIT out of MOVING EARTH and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A mangrove is a tropical tree or shrub that grows in salty coastal swamps, its roots arching above the mud.

clue.text: Charges having put stone foundation all around

indicators.note: turning all around makes the whole string face the other way, so it is read backwards

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British unit of weight
a bed is a base layer or foundation, as in a bed of concrete

explanation.surface: A builder bills for laying a stone foundation all the way around a house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' looks like a builder's fees; it is the definition in the sense of sums owed.
explanation.definitionFit: Charges are amounts billed to someone, and until paid these sums are debts they owe.

clue.text: Group in which Gary Barlow's first played piano

indicators.note: in which says the following letters go inside the group word

parts.note: a band is a musical group

indicators.note: played suggests the letters are performed in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of the singer's surname is used

parts.note: the opening letter of Barlow

explanation.surface: Gary Barlow, of the boy band Take That, played the piano in his first group.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is true to life: Gary Barlow is Take That's pianist and songwriter, which makes 'Group' look like a reference to the band.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby grand is a small grand piano, so it is a type of the general instrument named.

clue.text: Birds, loud feathered creatures below climber

indicators.note: in a down clue below means placed underneath, so the other pieces follow the climber

parts.note: a sweet pea or garden pea is a climbing plant
F is forte, the musical direction for loud
owls are feathered birds of prey

explanation.surface: Noisy birds roost beneath a mountaineer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' suggests a mountaineer, but it is a climbing plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Peafowl is the name for peacocks and peahens together, so the plural refers to these large pheasant-family birds.

clue.text: We heard tree grew money

indicators.note: what we heard is what reached our ears, so the words are taken by sound not spelling

parts.note: a yew is an evergreen tree
something that grew rose up

explanation.surface: Someone reports that a money tree has sprouted, the dream of every gardener.
explanation.definitionFit: Euros are the currency of most European Union countries, so they are money in the plural.

clue.text: Marital operations backfired, common to be disheartened

indicators.note: something that backfires goes backwards, so the operations word is read from the end

parts.note: ops is short for operations

indicators.note: disheartened means losing its heart, so the middle letter of the common word goes

parts.note: common and usual both mean ordinary

explanation.surface: A couple's schemes went wrong, as is usual when a marriage loses heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Spousal relates to a spouse, a husband or wife, so it is an adjective about married life.

clue.text: One hates novelty decoration on mobile phone

indicators.note: in an across clue on means placed after, so the decoration follows
mobile means able to move, so the letters of phone move around

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the Order of the British Empire, an honour awarded in Britain

explanation.surface: Someone who hates novelty objects to a fancy decoration stuck on a mobile phone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile phone' reads as one item, but 'mobile' is the anagram signal working on 'phone'.
explanation.definitionFit: A neophobe fears or dislikes anything new; the Greek roots mean new and fear, so a hater of novelty.

clue.text: Thief from Irish province left to the south after hour

indicators.note: in a down clue south is further down, so the left letter is moved lower within the word
after places the province word behind the hour letter

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hour
Ulster is the northern province of Ireland
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A thief from Ulster headed south an hour later.
explanation.walkthrough: The L of ULSTER moves two places down the word, giving USTLER.
explanation.definitionFit: A hustler is a swindler who cheats people out of money, so a kind of thief in the informal sense.

clue.text: Do this where salt is found acceptable?

definitions.text: Do this where salt is found acceptable?

parts.note: salt is crossword slang for a sailor, and sailors are found on the seas
on means acceptable, as in that's not on

explanation.surface: A cook asks whether to add a little more seasoning if salt is allowed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: you add salt when you season food. Read cryptically, salts (sailors) are found on the seas.
explanation.definitionFit: To season food is to flavour it, and salt is the commonest seasoning, so the whole question describes the verb.

clue.text: Taste fifty fancy sandwiches

indicators.note: a sandwich holds its filling between its slices, so the fancy word encloses the fifty letter

parts.note: to fancy something is to favour it
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone samples fifty elaborate sandwiches at a tasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy sandwiches' reads as food; 'fancy' is a verb and 'sandwiches' the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Taste and flavour are synonyms for the quality food has on the tongue, its savour.

clue.text: State of fear concocted with soldiers

parts.note: à la, on a menu, means cooked or prepared in a given style
RM is the Royal Marines, British commandos

explanation.surface: Panic is whipped up among a group of soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concocted' looks like an anagram signal, but the phrase is the menu term meaning prepared in a style.
explanation.definitionFit: Alarm is sudden fear or anxiety on sensing danger, so it is a state of fright.

clue.text: Dish of rabbit set back in aisle

indicators.note: in places the turned word inside the aisle word

parts.note: an aisle or narrow passage is a lane

indicators.note: something set back is turned to face the other way, so the chatter word is read backwards

parts.note: to rabbit is British slang for to chatter, and gas is idle talk

explanation.surface: A rabbit casserole is left out in the supermarket aisle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit' looks like the dish's meat; in British slang to rabbit on is to talk endlessly, which is also to gas.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasagne is an Italian baked dish of layered pasta sheets with sauce, served as a meal.

clue.text: One developing popular valved masks

indicators.note: a mask covers a face, so the words conceal the solution inside them

parts.note: inside popuLAR VAlved

explanation.surface: A developing trumpeter hides behind a popular brass instrument with valves.
explanation.definitionFit: A larva is an insect in its immature stage, still growing towards its adult form, like a caterpillar.

clue.text: Be in Dunstable, Derby etc and do multiple roles

definitions.meaning: a Dunstable is a straw hat and a derby a bowler hat, so being in them all means having several on in turn
an idiom for holding more than one job at once

explanation.surface: Someone tours English towns, Dunstable and Derby among them, taking on lots of different jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: Dunstable (a Bedfordshire town) and Derby (a Midlands city) look like places to visit; both are also kinds of hat.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom pictures changing headgear for each job, so someone juggling several positions or duties is said to do this.

clue.text: Clearly not on, electronic game with plug away

indicators.note: not tells us the following little word is absent from the game's name

parts.note: Simon is an electronic memory game with four coloured buttons
taken as written: the letters to remove
to ply a trade is to work steadily at it, to plug away

explanation.surface: An electronic game clearly won't switch on when someone has pulled out its plug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plug away' looks like unplugging the game; it is the idiom for working persistently.
explanation.definitionFit: Simply and clearly both mean plainly or in a straightforward way, as in put it simply.

clue.text: Dragon badly cut bottom after retreating

indicators.note: after places the turned word behind the trimmed one
cut means trimmed short, so the word for badly loses its last letter

parts.note: hard means badly, as in hard hit or hard done by

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the bottom word is read in reverse

parts.note: the nadir is the lowest point, the bottom

explanation.surface: A dragon badly wounded on its rear limps back to its lair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dragon' suggests a fire-breathing beast; it is the old insult for a fierce, bossy woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A dragon in this informal sense is a fierce, domineering older woman, which is exactly what harridan describes.
